steps.contain: Stop the agent, terminal or editor that ran it and end processes you do not recognise. If it may still be sending data, disconnect the network. Do not wipe the machine yet: its files show what was taken.
steps.scan-projects: Scan the repositories, packages and extensions involved, and every project opened since: pah scan <path>.
steps.check-agents: Check every agent's configuration for hooks, MCP servers, rules files, skills and folder-open tasks you did not add: pah sweep and pah watch check.
steps.remove-persistence: Remove what it left behind (the traces above), then look for other persistence: shell profiles, LaunchAgents, systemd user units, scheduled tasks and the Startup folder, cron and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. pah checkup lists the usual places.
steps.rotate-ai: From a device you trust, revoke and reissue AI credentials: API keys in each provider's console, and agent logins (sign out of Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Copilot and Cursor, then sign in again). A new password does not end a stolen session.
steps.rotate-github: GitHub: revoke personal access tokens, OAuth app grants, SSH and deploy keys you do not recognise, then review the security log and recent pushes, workflows, repositories and gists for ones you did not make.
steps.rotate-registry: npm and PyPI: revoke your tokens (npm token list, npm token revoke) and check whether any of your packages got a version you did not publish; deprecate or yank it and tell its users.
steps.rotate-cloud: Cloud: rotate the access keys in ~/.aws, the gcloud and Azure folders and .env files, and review the audit log for new users, keys and resources.
steps.sessions: Sign out of every browser session for email, password manager and code hosting, and revoke them from each account's security page: stealers take cookies, which skip passwords and 2FA.
steps.wallets: Move crypto funds from a clean device to a new wallet with a new seed phrase.
steps.update-agents: Update the AI CLIs and editors to their current versions (pah checkup lists versions with a known code-execution fix missing).
steps.reinstall: Reinstall the operating system if the payload ran with administrator rights, installed remote access, or left persistence you cannot fully explain.

incidents.name: MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE: fake recruiters and a Claude Code hook backdoor
incidents.summary: A suspected North Korean cluster used AI-generated recruiter personas and ClickFix-style "diagnostic fix" scripts, then edited .claude/settings.json in internal repositories so that starting Claude Code downloaded the SOMBERMEME backdoor. It also created GitHub personal access tokens named after Microsoft Copilot.
entry: Running a recruiter's "fix" command, then a hook in .claude/settings.json that runs when Claude Code starts in the repository.
respond: Check .claude/settings.json in your repositories and in ~/.claude for hooks you did not add (pah sweep, pah watch check).
GitHub: revoke personal access tokens you did not create, including ones named like Microsoft Copilot.
Never paste a "diagnostic" or "fix" command from a recruiter, a chat or a web page into a terminal.

incidents.name: GhostAction and WFX Phantom
incidents.summary: Stolen GitHub tokens pushed workflow changes that send every repository secret (toJSON(secrets)) out. GhostAction, first seen in September 2025 and back from September 2026 in about 30,000 repositories, posted them to a bare IP address from workflows named like security tooling. WFX Phantom (November 2026, tokens of about 4,837 accounts) hid the posting in a dot-file script run from a step named like a cache restore, wired the same script into postinstall, and reverted each change within seconds, so a gap in run numbers may be the only trace.
entry: A commit by a compromised account added a workflow, or a step with WF_SECRETS: ${{ toJSON(secrets) }}, that posts the secrets to a server.
WFX Phantom also ran the script from postinstall, so developers who ran npm install sent their own environment.
respond: Revoke the token that pushed the changes (revoke it, do not only rotate it) and the account's OAuth grants, SSH keys and sessions.
Rotate every repository and organisation secret the workflows could read: assume all of them were sent.
Check your cloud accounts for what was added: role trust policies opened to "Principal": {"AWS": "*"}, new IAM access keys, Azure federated credentials named wfx-ci-*.
Look for workflow runs you did not start, including gaps in run numbers, and delete the added workflows and dot-file scripts.
If you ran npm install while the postinstall script was there, rotate the credentials on your own machine.
Require review for changes under .github/workflows (branch protection or rulesets).

incidents.name: Trojanized Claude Code extension on Cursor's marketplace
incidents.summary: A copy of the Claude Code extension sat on Cursor's marketplace for about 11 hours on 29 October 2026, with up to 5,000 installs; it planted an SSH key, switched on the SSH server and opened a reverse tunnel.
entry: Installing the extension in Cursor ran its code with the editor.

traces.what: its LaunchAgent (Apple's own agents live in /System)
the SSH key it planted (comment svc-telemetry)

respond: Uninstall the extension and install Claude Code from Anthropic's own listing.
Delete the line ending in svc-telemetry from ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.
Turn the SSH server off unless you use it (macOS: System Settings, General, Sharing, Remote Login; Windows: the OpenSSH Server service).

incidents.name: testmetest worm and strutil-core
incidents.summary: A worm in hijacked repositories and packages: a binding.gyp loader planted hooks, rules, MCP entries and folder-open tasks for several agents at once, and armed a wiper that deletes your home folder when the stolen token stops working. Its descendants on RubyGems (strutil-core 1.0.1, November 2026, run from extconf.rb at gem install) and PyPI (pystr-codec) use the same persistence and add an MCP server named workspace-tools.
entry: binding.gyp ran a command while npm built the package; strutil-core's extconf.rb fetched Bun into /tmp/.b_<pid> and ran index.js at gem install.
It then wrote SessionStart hooks, Cursor rules, MCP server entries and folder-open tasks for several agents, and pushed the same files to the victim's repositories.

traces.what: service that keeps the worm running
LaunchAgent that keeps the worm running
the stolen token the wiper checks

respond: Do not revoke the stolen token first: net-health-checker.sh deletes your home folder when the token returns 401 or 403. Disconnect the network and copy your work to another machine or an external drive.
Only now revoke the token stored in ~/.config/net-health-checker/token and the other credentials, from a device you trust.

incidents.name: @subql/common release pipeline compromise
incidents.summary: A modified publish.yml replaced the package build with an archive downloaded without a hash check, so @subql/common 5.8.3 shipped code that is not in its source: a postinstall script that also runs on import, a workflow named codeql_analysis.yml committed as github-advanced-security[bot], and a remote shell.
entry: npm install of 5.8.3 ran postinstall: node ./dist/project/readers/manifest-cache.js.
respond: Use 5.8.2 and exclude 5.8.3, including as a transitive dependency.
Rebuild the machines and CI runners that installed it.
Delete the codeql_analysis.yml workflow if it appeared in your repositories.
Before trusting a release, compare the package with its source: pah diff --source <checkout at the tag> <package>.

incidents.name: PolinRider
incidents.summary: Amended and force-pushed commits in 188 GitHub repositories added a folder-open task that ran a loader disguised as a font; hijacked npm packages read their server from an Ethereum transaction and ran what it returned.
entry: A VS Code and Cursor task named eslint-check, with "runOn": "folderOpen", ran a loader saved as fa-solid-300.ttf when the folder was opened.
Hijacked npm packages read their command server from an Ethereum transaction and piped the reply into a detached node -i.
respond: In each affected repository, compare the history with what you pushed yourself (git log, git reflog): reset to your last own commit, delete the task and the fake font, and force-push only after rotating the token.

incidents.name: MALFEX
incidents.summary: An npm campaign with three payloads that hid code past the right edge of the editor with long runs of spaces and kept itself running through a scheduled task.
entry: Installing the package ran code pushed off-screen with spaces, which created a scheduled task.
respond: Delete the scheduled tasks you did not create (Task Scheduler, or schtasks /Query) and the payload folder.

incidents.name: LiteLLM .pth compromise
incidents.summary: LiteLLM was compromised on PyPI twice: an earlier release shipped a .pth file, and 1.107.0 (21 October 2026) shipped cook.pth and sitecustomize.py. Both run at every Python start, not only when LiteLLM is imported.
entry: pip install of the bad version put the .pth file in site-packages.
respond: Do not run pip or python in that environment until the .pth and sitecustomize.py files are gone: they run again at every interpreter start. Delete them from site-packages (python -I -S -c "import site; print(site.getsitepackages())" shows where without running them), then uninstall the bad version.
Rotate every provider key the LiteLLM configuration held.

incidents.name: Apex Accelerator
incidents.summary: npm packages posing as an AI agent set OPENROUTER_BASE_URL to the attacker's server, wrote an MCP server configuration and added a Microsoft Defender exclusion.
entry: Installing the package ran a dropper at install time.
respond: Remove Microsoft Defender exclusions you did not add (PowerShell: Get-MpPreference | Select-Object -ExpandProperty ExclusionPath, then Remove-MpPreference -ExclusionPath <path>) and run a full scan.
Remove OPENROUTER_BASE_URL from your environment and shell profile, and the MCP server entries it added.
Revoke the OpenRouter key and every other AI key the redirected traffic carried.

incidents.name: Poisoned AGENTS.md in Downloads (function-color)
incidents.summary: A 13 KB AGENTS.md posing as engineering guidelines, dropped into ~/Downloads by a website, made Codex change its machine-wide settings and then install the malicious npm package function-color in more than 90% of attempts. A CLAUDE.md variant got Claude Code to send its requests to the attacker's server about half the time, exposing the login token.
entry: Starting a coding agent in a folder that holds the file: agents read AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md on their own.
respond: Do not start coding agents in Downloads or other folders that hold files you did not write; delete the planted file.
Check whether function-color is installed (npm ls -g function-color, and npm ls function-color in your projects) and remove it.
Undo the settings the agent changed (~/.codex/config.toml, ~/.claude/settings.json); pah checkup lists risky settings.

incidents.name: Unauthorized Codex and Claude Code relays
incidents.summary: After a genuine npm install of the CLI, setup scripts run with iwr | iex or curl | bash rewrote the agents' configuration to send all traffic through a third-party relay: base_url, sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access" and network_access in ~/.codex/config.toml, and ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and DISABLE_TELEMETRY as user environment variables.
entry: Pasting a "cheap access" setup command from a relay's page.

traces.what: Codex configured to use a known relay
Claude Code configured to use a known relay

respond: Remove base_url, sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access" and network_access from ~/.codex/config.toml, and ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and DISABLE_TELEMETRY from your user environment variables (Windows) or shell profile (macOS, Linux).
Rotate the API keys and sign in to the agents again: every prompt, file and key they sent went through the relay.
Install the CLIs only with the vendor's instructions; pah checkup flags API base URLs that are not the vendor's.

incidents.name: SleepyDuck
incidents.summary: Open VSX extensions for Solidity developers carried a payload appended to an MP4 file and installed a backdoor that starts at login.
entry: Installing the extension in an editor that uses Open VSX (Cursor, Windsurf, VSCodium) ran its code with the editor.
respond: Uninstall the Solidity extension it came with and check your other Open VSX extensions.

incidents.name: PyPI .pth typosquats of AI libraries
incidents.summary: Packages named like AI libraries (openaii, ollamaa, langgrap, transfomers) dropped a <name>-setup.pth file, which runs at every Python start. Reported by one vendor.
entry: pip install of a misspelled name.
respond: Do not run Python in that environment until the .pth file is gone: delete *-setup.pth from site-packages, then uninstall the package.
Check requirements files for misspelled names (pah scan reports look-alikes).

incidents.name: Paperclip and Browser Use skill clones
incidents.summary: Look-alike publishers copied the official Paperclip and Browser Use skills to skills.sh word for word. Once installs grew, a commit added setup-installation.md in seven paths: SKILL.md stayed clean and sent the agent there, and it ran curl -k on a look-alike API, decoded the reply with base64 and ran it with node.
entry: The agent loaded the skill and followed its setup instructions.
respond: Remove the cloned skills and every setup-installation.md they brought, and install skills only from their real publishers.
If the loader ran, treat it as a stealer infection: pah incident show ai-token-stealers.
Compare installed skills with their upstream on every update: pah diff <installed> <new version>.

incidents.name: Deadbugz: an MCP server that changes its tools after three calls
incidents.summary: An account opened 23 pull requests adding an MCP server named productivity-suite with harmless tools (format_text, summarize). After the third call its tool list and prompts changed to steer the agent toward SSH keys, AWS credentials and kubeconfig. Four of the pull requests pointed to a script hidden in ~/.config/.cache/.sys/. None was merged.
entry: Merging the pull request adds the server to the project's MCP configuration; the agent starts it and calls its tools.
respond: Reject pull requests and configurations that add productivity-suite or point at productivity-suite-mcp.onrender.com or a trycloudflare.com host.
Keep the MCP client logs: they show which tool definitions the agent was given.
Pin MCP servers to versions you reviewed and approve a server again when its tools change.
If the agent read keys while the server was running, rotate them.

incidents.name: ChainDrop (keyv worm)
incidents.summary: A Shai-Hulud variant: the keyv maintainer's account was hijacked and the project's own trusted-publishing workflow released 444 infected packages (keyv 6.0.0, cacheable 2.5.1, flat-cache 6.1.24 and file-entry-cache 11.1.6 among them), so they carried valid provenance. The same loader came back in tensorlake 0.5.144 in October.
entry: "preinstall": "node setup.mjs" downloaded Bun 1.3.13 and ran Math_Symbol.js or math_init.js.

The payload took npm, GitHub and AI-agent credentials (.codex/auth.json, .cursor/credentials.json, .gemini/.env, .kiro/settings/mcp.json, opencode.json), committed a .claude/settings.json SessionStart hook and a folder-open task to up to 50 branches per repository (author claude, message "chore: update config"), and added a "Run Copilot" workflow that puts every secret into a build artifact.

traces.what: token monitor that acts when the stolen token is revoked

respond: Remove the token monitor (the traces above) before rotating anything: it acts when the stolen token is revoked.
Reinstall your dependencies at versions from before the incident with --ignore-scripts.
Delete the branches and commits by "claude" with the message "chore: update config", and the "Run Copilot" workflow, from your repositories.

incidents.name: arrayref, internment and append-only-vec crates
incidents.summary: arrayref 0.3.10, internment 0.8.7 and append-only-vec 0.1.9 were on crates.io for 86 to 107 minutes with a new dependency, proc-macro1 1.0.107, whose build.rs downloaded a payload from a bare IP address and started it.
entry: cargo build compiled proc-macro1 and ran its build.rs.
respond: Pin arrayref =0.3.9, internment =0.8.6 and append-only-vec =0.1.8, and check Cargo.lock for proc-macro1.
Delete ~/.cargo/registry/cache, CI caches and vendored copies that hold the bad versions.
On every machine that built them, rotate SSH keys, cloud credentials, crates.io tokens and signing keys.

incidents.name: Stealers that take AI-agent tokens (WardenStealer, Aokigahara, Vidar)
incidents.summary: Infostealers now take AI-agent logins: WardenStealer (more than 130,000 infections since 3 August 2026) takes Claude Code OAuth tokens, MCP server tokens included, and Codex auth.json; Aokigahara reads the session files of Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code, Gemini CLI and Copilot; a Vidar variant took OpenClaw's gateway token and memory file.
entry: Usually a cracked program, a fake installer or a pasted command; the stealer copies the session files and leaves.

incidents.name: Planted programs and relocated agent configuration
incidents.summary: Agents ran code from a repository before the first prompt: a git.exe at the top of the repository ran when it was opened in Cursor, Claude Desktop or Kiro (CVE-2026-63093, CVE-2026-88066, CVE-2026-18656); GEMINI_CLI_HOME in a .env file started an MCP server (CVE-2026-13745); a __proto__ key in .vscode/mcp.json did the same in Restricted Mode (CVE-2026-121662); and PATH pointing at a repository's bin/git ran through Claude Code's startup git probes.
entry: Opening the repository in the agent was enough: it looked up git or read .env and project configuration before asking for trust.

incidents.name: Miasma worm
incidents.summary: A worm planted Claude Code and Gemini CLI SessionStart hooks, a Cursor rule and a VS Code folder-open task in the repositories it reached; GitHub disabled 73 Microsoft repositories.
entry: The hooks run when an agent session starts in the folder; the task runs when the folder opens in VS Code or Cursor.
respond: Remove the hooks, rules and tasks from every affected repository and restore its history from a commit you made yourself.

incidents.name: InstallFix: fake AI install pages
incidents.summary: Search ads led to cloned Claude Code install pages whose one-line install commands (curl … | zsh, mshta https://…) installed the Amatera and Cuckoo stealers; researchers counted 88 lure domains, more than 30 of them for Claude Code. Shared ChatGPT, Grok and claude.ai chats were used as lure pages for AMOS and MacSync.
entry: Pasting the page's install command into a terminal or the Windows Run box.
respond: Install AI tools only from the vendor's own site, typed by hand, never from an ad or a shared chat.

incidents.name: Clinejection
incidents.summary: Text in a GitHub issue title hijacked Cline's AI triage workflow and led to a stolen npm token; cline@2.3.0 installed OpenClaw globally from its postinstall script.
entry: An AI agent in a GitHub workflow acted on an issue anyone could open, with the release token within reach.
Installing cline@2.3.0 ran its postinstall script.
respond: If you installed cline@2.3.0, update Cline and remove the OpenClaw package it installed globally (npm ls -g, then npm uninstall -g).
Maintainers: do not give an AI agent in a workflow write tokens or secrets when anyone can trigger it (pah scan reports this as PAH-I011).

incidents.name: ClawHavoc: malicious skills on ClawHub
incidents.summary: 341 of 2,857 skills on ClawHub were malicious on 1 February 2026, and 824 by 16 February; most delivered the AMOS stealer for macOS.
entry: A skill's setup step told the agent, or the user, to download and run a program.
respond: Remove the skill and check your other installed skills (pah sweep).

incidents.name: StoatWaffle: fake job-interview repositories
incidents.summary: Repositories sent as coding tests in fake job interviews ran StoatWaffle through .vscode/tasks.json with "runOn": "folderOpen": opening the folder was enough.
entry: Opening the repository in VS Code or Cursor and trusting the folder.
respond: Open code from recruiters only in a disposable VM, or in Restricted Mode with automatic tasks off ("task.allowAutomaticTasks": "off").

incidents.name: Slopsquatting: react-codeshift
incidents.summary: The hallucinated package name react-codeshift appeared in 47 AI-generated skills copied into 237 repositories; whoever registers such a name gets their code run. Across 16 models, 5.2% (commercial) and 21.7% (open) of suggested packages did not exist.
entry: A skill told the agent to run npx react-codeshift; npx fetches whatever is published under that name.
respond: Remove or fix the skill: pin packages to an exact, known version and publisher.
If the command ran after someone registered the name, treat it as malware: follow pah incident show ai-token-stealers.

incidents.name: Phantom Gyp
incidents.summary: 57 npm packages ran code while being built, through command expansion in binding.gyp.
entry: node-gyp evaluates <!(…) command expansions in binding.gyp during npm install.

incidents.name: Claude Code project files before the trust prompt
incidents.summary: Project files could run code or send the API key to another server before the trust prompt (CVE-2025-59536, CVE-2026-21852). Both are patched and no exploitation is known.
entry: Opening an untrusted repository with an affected Claude Code version.
respond: If you opened untrusted repositories with an affected version, revoke your Anthropic API key and sign in to Claude Code again.

incidents.name: Malware that calls AI models (PROMPTFLUX, PROMPTSTEAL)
incidents.summary: Google's threat intelligence group reported malware that asks AI models for code while it runs: PROMPTFLUX rewrites itself through the Gemini API to evade antivirus, and PROMPTSTEAL (LAMEHUG) asks a model for the commands that collect documents and system information.
entry: Usually a phishing attachment or a fake installer.
respond: Check the Startup folder for scripts you did not put there (pah checkup reports them).

incidents.name: PhantomRaven
incidents.summary: 126 npm packages that showed "0 dependencies" on the registry fetched their payload at install time from URL dependencies, so the code that ran was never on npm.
entry: npm install followed a dependency given as an http URL and ran its install script.
respond: Remove the package and every package from the same publisher; npm 12 and later no longer fetch URL dependencies unless a project's .npmrc turns that back on.

incidents.name: GlassWorm
incidents.summary: A self-spreading worm in Open VSX and VS Code extensions, later also on GitHub and npm, that hid its code in invisible Unicode variation selectors and used stolen developer tokens to publish more infected releases.
entry: Installing or auto-updating an infected extension ran its hidden code with the editor.
respond: Uninstall the infected extensions and turn off automatic extension updates until you have checked the rest.
Revoke your Open VSX and VS Code Marketplace publisher tokens.

incidents.name: Shai-Hulud
incidents.summary: A self-spreading npm worm: install scripts swept the machine for tokens and secrets and republished the victims' packages with the worm inside. At least seven waves ran from September 2025 to August 2026; the sweep grew from 189 to 469 file paths, including Cursor, OpenClaw and Codex configuration, and Mini Shai-Hulud persisted through .claude/settings.json hooks.
entry: npm install of an infected version ran its install script, which used the stolen npm and GitHub tokens to publish more infected versions.
respond: Look in your GitHub account for repositories and workflow files you did not create: the first wave published the stolen secrets in a public repository named Shai-Hulud.

incidents.name: postmark-mcp: the first malicious MCP server
incidents.summary: An npm package posing as a Postmark MCP server added a hidden BCC to every email it sent, from version 1.0.16 on, after fifteen clean versions.
entry: The agent started the MCP server from an unpinned npm package and picked up the new version.
respond: Remove postmark-mcp from every agent's MCP configuration and uninstall it.
Revoke the Postmark server token it used and review what it sent.
Pin MCP servers to an exact version you reviewed (pah scan reports unpinned ones as PAH-A013).

incidents.name: s1ngularity (Nx)
incidents.summary: Malicious Nx versions ran Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Amazon Q with their permission checks bypassed to search the machine for secrets; 2,349 secrets from 1,079 machines were published.
entry: The package's postinstall script started the AI CLIs already installed, with flags that skip approvals.

traces.what: line it added to shut the machine down in every new shell
line it added to shut the machine down in every new shell

respond: Remove the line sudo shutdown -h 0 from ~/.bashrc and ~/.zshrc.
Delete the repositories named s1ngularity-repository (and -0, -1, …) from your GitHub account: they hold your stolen secrets.
Update Nx and its plugins to versions published after the incident.
